lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you read closely. What is an inference? Something you work out from clues in the text and from what you already know.
When you say something about a text, back it up. One quote might be chance; two or three pieces of evidence from different parts of the text make a strong case.

Evidence can be a quote, the author's exact words in quotation marks, or a paraphrase, the same idea in your own words. Quote only the key words: Mira 'gripped the rope' says more than a whole copied paragraph.
Choose the strongest evidence: it is relevant to your point and shows it clearly. 'She smiled' is weak proof that Mira is overjoyed; 'she laughed until tears came' is strong.

lines: Mira gripped the rope with both hands.
The bridge swayed over the deep gorge.
Knees shaking, she took one step, then another.
picture.title: Claim: Mira is brave

lesson.text: Then explain every piece: point, evidence, explain. Point: Mira is brave. Evidence: 'knees shaking, she took one step'. Explain: she is afraid, yet she keeps going.
Information texts need evidence too: say where a fact comes from. 'The guide says the river is 340 km long' is stronger than 'the river is very long'.
Try it in the world: read a sign or a book in the game and make a claim about it. Back it with two pieces of evidence and explain them. Next: how a theme develops.

choices: She says the night was quiet.
The night seemed calm to her.
exercises.hint: A quote copies the exact words inside quotation marks.
exercises.explain: "The night was still" is in quotation marks: the writer's exact words.

exercises.prompt: One quote is always enough to prove a big point about a text.
exercises.hint: Could one line be a one-off?
exercises.explain: False: two or three pieces from different parts of the text make a stronger case.

exercises.prompt: Claim: the old man is kind. Which line proves it best?
choices: He shared his bread with a stray dog.
exercises.hint: Which line shows how he treats others?
exercises.explain: Sharing his bread shows kindness; his hat and his home say nothing about it.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: a quote or a paraphrase?
items: She says the wind was loud.
He says the sea never rests.
exercises.hint: Look for quotation marks round exact words.
exercises.explain: Quotes keep the exact words in quotation marks; paraphrases put the idea in new words.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a paragraph to its job.
matches: a quote that backs it up
exercises.hint: First say it, then show it, then say how it shows it.
exercises.explain: Point: what you claim. Evidence: a quote that backs it up. Explain: how the quote proves the point.

exercises.prompt: Claim: the forest is dangerous. Which evidence is relevant?
choices: Wolves howled close to the path.
exercises.hint: Which line would make a reader feel unsafe?
exercises.explain: Wolves close by show danger; tall trees and the season do not.

exercises.prompt: Build the paragraph in the right order.
items: Giving all he has shows he puts others first.
He gives his last coin to a stranger.
exercises.hint: Point first, then the evidence, then the explanation.
exercises.explain: The point (Leo is generous), the evidence (his last coin), then what the evidence shows.

exercises.prompt: Claim: Tom feels left out. Which evidence is strongest?
exercises.hint: Which line shows how Tom gets on with others?
exercises.explain: "No one sat with Tom, again" shows he is often left alone; the others say nothing about it.

exercises.prompt: Claim: Tom is kind. Sort the lines.
items: He cheered up a crying boy.
exercises.hint: Does the line show Tom doing something kind?
exercises.explain: Supports it: sharing his lunch, carrying the bags, cheering up the boy. The others say nothing about kindness.

exercises.hint: Whose words are in a paraphrase?
exercises.explain: False: a paraphrase is in your own words, so it has no quotation marks.

exercises.prompt: Which quote is trimmed best to prove that Kit is clever?
choices: Kit "mended the radio with a hairpin".
exercises.hint: Keep only the words that prove the point.
exercises.explain: "mended the radio with a hairpin" is short and proves cleverness; the others prove nothing.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to its evidence.
exercises.explain: Climbing the cliff shows bravery; solving the riddle shows cleverness; sharing her map shows kindness.

exercises.prompt: What do the two marked pieces of evidence show together?
exercises.hint: Compare Jun at the start with Jun at the end.
exercises.explain: At first Jun hides; by the end he speaks up. Together they show him growing braver.

lines: Jun hid behind his books all term.
At the meeting he stood up and spoke.
picture.title: Claim: Jun changes

exercises.prompt: Two quotes seem to disagree: Mira 'trembled', yet she 'stepped forward'. What should you do?
choices: Use both: she is afraid but brave.
exercises.hint: Can both be true at once?
exercises.explain: Use both: being afraid yet going on anyway is exactly what bravery is.

exercises.prompt: Order the evidence from the weakest to the strongest for: Ana loves the sea.
exercises.hint: The strongest shows her feelings in her own words.
exercises.explain: Living near it proves little; swimming often is better; her own words about being happiest are the strongest.

exercises.prompt: Which line cites an information text best?
choices: The guide says the bridge is 60 m long.
The bridge is long, I think.
Everyone knows the bridge is long.
exercises.hint: Good citing names the source and gives the exact fact.
exercises.explain: It names the source, the guide, and gives an exact figure; the others give no source and no fact.

exercises.prompt: Match each weak spot to its fix.
exercises.hint: For each problem, what would make the case stronger?
exercises.explain: One quote: add more evidence. A long quote: trim it to the key words. No explanation: explain it. Off-topic: pick a relevant line.

exercises.prompt: Claim: the storm frightens the crew. Sort the lines.
items: "I've never been so scared," said Bo.
exercises.hint: Does the line say the fear in words, show it in actions, or say nothing about it?
exercises.explain: Outright: the two spoken lines. Hints: the silence and the pale captain. Not evidence: the masts and the season.

exercises.prompt: Evidence from the start and the end of a story can show how a character changes.
exercises.hint: Change means a difference between two points in time.
exercises.explain: True: comparing early and late evidence shows the change.
